Presidential Spokesperson and Minister of Government Communications, Felix Kwakye Ofosu, has cited former President Nana Akufo-Addo’s criticism of a previous government’s decision to acquire an executive jet to defend the Mahama administration’s purchase of a new Falcon 6X aircraft.
Speaking on JoyNews ’ The Pulse on Tuesday, November 17, Mr Kwakye Ofosu said opposition to government decisions to acquire presidential aircraft was not new, pointing to comments made by Nana Akufo-Addo, then the Minority Ranking Member of Foreign Affairs in Parliament in February 2000.
He said Nana Akufo-Addo had criticised Jerry John Rawlings' administration’s planned purchase of a Gulfstream III aircraft, arguing that the expenditure was inconsistent with the country’s economic and social priorities.
Reading from the February 15, 2000 edition of the Parliamentary Hansard, Mr Kwakye Ofosu quoted Nana Akufo-Addo as saying that at a time when the country needed greater public investment in health and tertiary education, the government was considering spending $19 million over five years on an aircraft for the President.
“If anything demonstrates the need that has been consistently urged from this side of the House for us to review and prioritise public expenditure, this case justifies that call. I have no doubt, Mr Speaker, that if the priorities are spelt out properly, the purchase of an executive jet will come very low down on the scale of priorities,” Mr Akufo-Addo was quoted as saying.
"So, this is President Akufo-Addo assailing the Rawlings government for planning to buy the Gulfstream three aircraft," the Presidential Spokesperson added.
Mr Kwakye Ofosu said the opposition to the aircraft purchase continued after the New Patriotic Party (NPP) assumed office under former President John Agyekum Kufuor.
He claimed that former President Kufuor did not use the aircraft during his eight years in office and that a three-member committee was set up to investigate the purchase and found no evidence of wrongdoing.
"Indeed, they did not limit their opposition to that aircraft to just criticism. When they won power, and President Akufo-Addo became foreign minister, President Kufour refused to use that jet for eight years. They even went on and fabricated claims of corruption in the purchase of that aircraft."
"So, they set up a three-member committee chaired by the late J.H. Mensa, which had then Finance Minister Mr. Osafo Marfo and Kwabena Agyapong, then presidential spokesperson as members to look into the purchase. In fact, for eight years they found nothing.
"President Kuffour did not use that aircraft even once. So, it sat down, deteriorated, and then they exchanged," he said.
Mr Kwakye Ofosu argued that the historical opposition to the purchase of an executive jet by the NPP did not provide sufficient grounds to criticise the current administration over its acquisition of the Falcon 6X.
"So Honorable Ablakwa criticizing President Akufo-Addo for decisions that were inconsistent with the economic realities of the Ghanaian at the time is no basis upon which somebody sees to criticize this today," he said.
He also distinguished the circumstances surrounding the two purchases, saying the Mahama administration inherited an economy that had been severely weakened by the previous government.
According to him, the country was grappling with high inflation, a rapidly depreciating cedi and debt challenges, while government had struggled to meet its obligations to bondholders and pensioners.

He cited the participation of former Chief Justice Sophia Akuffo in demonstrations by pensioners demanding payment of their investments as an indication of the economic difficulties at the time.
"In that circumstance, we cannot say that you're going to buy a presidential jet. That also came on the back of a decision by the administration to rent expensive jets when the presidential jet was not available."
He criticised the previous administration's decision to rent expensive jets when the presidential aircraft was unavailable, saying that "If you needed to fly at a time when the jet was not available, there were other affordable options.
"So, you could rent a more modest jet or could go commercial as President Mahama has done."
